title: Log Loss
body:
[[Logistic Regression]]

---

$$
L = -\big[y\log q + (1-y)\log(1-q)\big]
$$

The [[Binary Classification]] loss: $y \in \{0,1\}$ is the true label, $q$ is the model's predicted
$P(y=1)$. One of the two terms is always zero, so it reduces to $-\log(\text{probability given to
the right answer})$. Also called binary cross-entropy.

**It is [[Cross-Entropy Loss]] with $k = 2$**, and that note owns the derivation, the gradient
argument, and why squared error is the wrong choice here. What this note adds is the *other* route
to the same formula, which is where the name comes from.

## The likelihood derivation

[[Logistic Regression]] models each label as a [[Bernoulli Distribution]] with parameter $q$, so
the probability of observing the whole dataset is

$$
\prod_i q_i^{y_i}(1-q_i)^{1-y_i}
$$

Maximum likelihood says pick the [[Weights]] that make that product largest. Products of many
small numbers underflow and do not differentiate pleasantly, so take the log, which turns the
product into a sum and is monotone so the maximiser is unchanged. Then negate, because optimisers
minimise. What falls out is the sum of the formula above, hence **log** loss.

So the same function arrives twice: as expected code length ([[Information Theory]]) and as
negative log likelihood (statistics). That is not a coincidence, and it is the tidiest example in
the vault of the two subjects being the same subject.
